scenario: A new team plans to design its first Azure workload from a blank whiteboard, using a blog post from 2019 for inspiration.
stem: What is the better starting point?
options: The closest reference architecture in the Azure Architecture Center, with each deviation recorded as a decision
The newest blog post they can find
Whatever the most senior engineer used last time
A design with every Azure service that might be useful later
explanation: Reference architectures are maintained, reasoned and often deployable. Starting from one turns the review into a discussion of deviations. Old posts and habits carry outdated assumptions.

scenario: Five developers propose fourteen microservices on AKS for a product launching in four months.
stem: What is the strongest argument against it?
options: AKS cannot run fourteen services
Microservices are always slower
Microservices solve a many-teams problem and add distributed-systems work; one team is better served by a modular monolith that can be split later
Microservices cannot use Azure SQL
explanation: The benefit of microservices is independent delivery by separate teams. With one team, you pay the costs - network calls, consistency, contracts, operations - without that benefit.

stem: What makes a monolith 'modular' in a useful sense?
options: It runs in containers
Strict internal boundaries: each module owns its logic and schema and talks to others only through defined interfaces, so it can be extracted later
It has one large shared database that every module writes to freely
It is split into several repositories
explanation: The boundaries are the point. They keep today's system simple to run while leaving the option to extract a service when a second team needs to own it. A shared, freely written schema removes that option.

scenario: An ASP.NET application runs on two on-premises servers. The business wants it on Azure within three months, with better reliability, and no rewrite.
options: Microservices on AKS
Baseline chat app
Multi-region active-active
The Reliable Web App pattern: managed PaaS services plus retries, circuit breakers, caching and managed identity with minimal code change
explanation: The Reliable Web App pattern is designed for exactly this move. A microservices rewrite would not fit three months, and multi-region is only justified by a requirement.

stem: Your design starts from the web app baseline but runs in one region instead of zone-redundant across zones and regions. What should happen?
options: Record the deviation, the reason (such as an accepted RTO) and the trade-off in an architecture decision record
Nothing; reference architectures are only suggestions
Hide it from the review so it passes
Add a second region anyway, to match
explanation: Deviations are often right, but they are decisions with consequences. An ADR stops the next reviewer from re-arguing them and makes the risk visible to the business.

scenario: In a review, the design saves an order to SQL and then publishes an 'order placed' event in a separate call.
stem: Which pattern should the reviewer ask about?
options: Cache-aside
Valet key
Transactional outbox, so the event is written in the same transaction and published reliably afterwards
Strangler fig
explanation: Two separate writes can disagree when one fails. The outbox pattern keeps the data and the event consistent. Naming the pattern makes the review question short and precise.

stem: Why does a baseline reference architecture cost much more than a starter design?
options: Architecture Center designs use premium support plans
It is production-grade: WAF, zone redundancy, private endpoints and premium tiers, so use it for production and a cut-down version for dev, with the difference written down
Baselines always include AKS
Reference architectures require an Enterprise Agreement
explanation: Each baseline component buys reliability or security for production. Dev rarely needs all of it, so cut deliberately, and record the difference so it is not a surprise at go-live.

scenario: Awarding points and sending welcome emails makes the loyalty API's sign-up request take eight seconds.
options: A bigger App Service plan
Microservices, one per email type
A second region
Web-queue-worker: the API puts the slow work on a queue and returns, and a worker processes it
explanation: Moving slow work off the request path makes the API responsive and lets the worker scale and retry on its own. A bigger plan makes the slow work only slightly faster.
